summary: Matt Brooks has run the Republican Jewish Coalition since 1990, turning a small Washington coalition into one of the Republican Party's most active donor and turnout organizations. Through its candidate forums, its PAC and the RJC Victory Fund super PAC he has directed money toward Republicans he considers reliably pro-Israel and against those he does not, including the $5 million effort that helped defeat Rep. Thomas Massie in Kentucky's May 2026 primary. A defender of Donald Trump's record on Israel since 2016, he has also publicly broken with Republicans and conservative institutions over antisemitism, most sharply with the Heritage Foundation in 2025.

chapters.title: A Reagan convert at Brandeis
chapters.dek: A Philadelphia Democrat's son who swapped medical school for Jack Kemp's campaign.
chapters.body:
Matt Brooks grew up in a family of politically active Democrats in Philadelphia. The family changed sides together in 1980: Brooks and his parents moved toward Ronald Reagan in a campaign he later summarized as the Iran hostages, long gas lines and "a horrible economy" under Jimmy Carter. [[brandeis-brooks-2022]]

At Brandeis University he was, in his own words, "the campus radical." Ahead of the 1984 election he organized the university's College Republicans, a chapter he says grew from three members to about 300, and he became state chairman of the Massachusetts College Republicans. [[brandeis-brooks-2022, rjc-brooks-bio]]

He was a political science major planning on medical school when a Brandeis-funded summer internship placed him in the House office of Jack Kemp. Kemp became the decisive patron. Brooks graduated in 1987, deferred medical school to work on Kemp's presidential campaign, and managed it in Massachusetts while directing projects in New Hampshire and New England. Kemp lost the 1988 nomination to George H.W. Bush, and Brooks never went back to medicine. [[toi-brooks-2019, brandeis-brooks-2022, rjc-brooks-bio]]

> He became my mentor, he was my rabbi, he was my friend, and he was somebody who had an incalculable impact of my life. [[toi-brooks-2019]]

chapters.title: From political director to the coalition's permanent operator
chapters.dek: Two years after joining, he was running the organization he still leads.
chapters.body:
The National Jewish Coalition had been founded in 1985 by senior Jewish Republicans; it later took the name Republican Jewish Coalition. Brooks joined as political director in 1988 and immediately took leave to serve as national field director of the Victory '88 Jewish Campaign Committee for the Bush-Quayle ticket. [[jvl-rjc, rjc-brooks-bio, toi-brooks-2019]]

In 1990 he became executive director. He has held the top staff job ever since, through chairmen including Cheryl Halpern, David Flaum and former senator Norm Coleman, the current national chairman. He also runs the Jewish Policy Center, the RJC's think tank, and finished a Georgetown MBA in 1996 while doing both. By 2024 his title had become chief executive officer. [[rjc-about, rjc-brooks-bio, ji-rjc-trump-2016, toi-rnc-2024]]

The job combines three functions that later chapters show in use: access, because the RJC's forums and summits are where Republican candidates meet Jewish donors; money, through the RJC PAC and later the RJC Victory Fund super PAC; and turnout programs aimed at Jewish voters in swing states. Brooks is also the group's principal spokesman. [[rjc-brooks-bio, religionwatch-rjc-2025, fec-rjc-victory-fund]]

chapters.title: Adelson money and the battleground Jewish vote
chapters.dek: A casino owner's patronage turned a coalition into a campaign operation.
chapters.body:
Sheldon Adelson's relationship with the RJC preceded his emergence as the largest Republican donor in the country. The coalition honored him at its 20th-anniversary luncheon in 2005, alongside Bernard Marcus and RNC chairman Ken Mehlman, and he sat on its board until his death. The organization's statement on that death, signed by Coleman and Brooks, called him a "dear mentor and friend." [[jvl-rjc, rjc-adelson-2021]]

The money paid for campaigns rather than conferences. In September 2012 the RJC began a $5 million television campaign featuring former Obama voters expressing "buyer's remorse," aimed at Florida, Nevada, Ohio and Pennsylvania, as part of a $6.5 million effort that JTA reported Adelson and other board members would fund. Earlier coverage had found no one willing to confirm Adelson's role, so the funding is recorded here as reported rather than settled. [[jta-ad-campaign-2012]]

Brooks also used the forum invitation as a gatekeeping tool. In December 2011 he excluded Ron Paul from the RJC's presidential forum, saying the group "rejects his misguided and extreme views." By April 2015 the RJC's spring meeting at Adelson's Venetian hotel was being called the "Sheldon primary" as Ted Cruz, Mike Pence and Rick Perry sought his support. Asked about the phrase, Brooks replied: "Who?" [[reason-ron-paul-2011, jta-adelson-2015]]

chapters.title: From an awkward forum to Trump's defense
chapters.dek: The coalition stayed quiet in the 2016 primary, then became one of Trump's most consistent Jewish defenders.
chapters.body:
Donald Trump's first appearance at an RJC forum, in December 2015, went badly. He told the audience, "You're not going to support me because I don't want your money," and was booed when he declined to say Jerusalem should be Israel's undivided capital. When Trump became the presumptive nominee in May 2016, the RJC's congratulatory statement, issued by chairman David Flaum, focused on Hillary Clinton's record rather than Trump's. [[jta-trump-forum-2015, ji-rjc-trump-2016]]

By 2019 Brooks was making the affirmative case. He predicted Trump would win more Jewish votes in 2020 than in 2016 and said that for voters who cared about Israel and national security "there's only one choice." When Trump said in August 2019 that Jewish Democratic voters showed disloyalty, the ADL called the remark antisemitic; the RJC tweeted "President Trump is right," and Brooks said the president was "not plowing any new fields." [[toi-brooks-2019, jta-disloyalty-2019]]

The 2020 campaign put money behind the argument: $10 million pledged to re-elect Trump and hold Congress, with paid field staff in Florida and targeting in Ohio, Arizona, Pennsylvania and Georgia. In 2022 Brooks still declined to criticize Trump for telling American Jews to "get their act together," pointing instead to the Jerusalem embassy move and the Abraham Accords. [[jta-swing-2020, brandeis-brooks-2022]]

chapters.title: Drawing lines inside the party
chapters.dek: Zero tolerance for antisemites, without breaking with Trump.
chapters.body:
Brooks's defense of Trump has coexisted with public breaks from other Republicans. In the 2022 midterms the RJC refused to support Pennsylvania gubernatorial nominee Doug Mastriano and worked to defeat Marjorie Taylor Greene; Brooks described the policy as "zero tolerance for antisemitism." [[brandeis-brooks-2022]]

The limit of that policy showed in November 2022, when Trump hosted Ye and the White nationalist Nick Fuentes at Mar-a-Lago. The coalition condemned the two guests as "virulent" antisemites and urged leaders to refuse such meetings, but did not name Trump. [[algemeiner-fuentes-2022, cbs-fuentes-2022]]

His sharpest break came in October 2025, after Heritage Foundation president Kevin Roberts defended Tucker Carlson's friendly interview with Fuentes. Brooks said he was "appalled, offended and disgusted," called the defense "a total abrogation" of Heritage's mission, and said the RJC would reassess a relationship that had included work with Heritage's foreign-policy team. He cast the dispute as factional: Heritage was becoming "more like Tucker Carlson and less like Ronald Reagan." [[ji-heritage-2025]]

chapters.title: The largest Jewish turnout campaign
chapters.dek: A convention speech, a $15 million program and a doubled budget.
chapters.body:
In July 2024 Brooks became the first RJC chief invited to address a Republican National Convention. He told delegates in Milwaukee that Trump would "bring back law and order" and "stop the mobs on college campuses," and told reporters afterward that "for the first time I can ever remember there is true insecurity in the Jewish community." He described Trump's call for Israel to finish the war against Hamas as a "blank check," not pressure. [[toi-rnc-2024, jns-rnc-2024]]

That September the RJC began a $10 million ad buy in Pennsylvania, Georgia, Nevada, Michigan and Arizona within a $15 million program that Brooks called "by far, the largest and most comprehensive effort ever to turn out the Jewish vote" for Trump. By the end of October the RJC's committees had raised more than $18 million since January 2023, including $5 million from Miriam Adelson and $2.4 million from Jan Koum; the super PAC alone had more than doubled its 2020 haul. [[ji-ad-buy-2024, forward-billionaires-2024]]

Across the cycle, the RJC PAC and super PAC spent about $20 million on Trump and Senate candidates in key states, twice the 2020 figure. Brooks has described the RJC's leverage in plain terms: the group either delivers money or delivers votes. The coalition's annual summit drew about 1,500 attendees, up from about 250 in 2010. The Dispatch, whose account is summarized here, also reported that Brooks recommended Mike Huckabee as ambassador to Israel. [[religionwatch-rjc-2025, dispatch-rjc-2025]]

chapters.title: Consequences: the Massie primary and the midterms
chapters.dek: For the first time, RJC money helped remove a sitting Republican.
chapters.body:
In the 2026 cycle Brooks turned the RJC's money against an incumbent Republican. Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky had voted against Israel aid and antisemitism resolutions and against several of Trump's priorities. The RJC and the RJC Victory Fund committed $5 million to Ed Gallrein, Trump's endorsed challenger, and Gallrein won the May 19 primary. Brooks said Massie had been "trafficking in antisemitism and bottom-of-the-barrel nativism" and that there was "no place in the Republican Party for those who turn their back on the MAGA agenda." The $5 million figure is the RJC's own. [[rjc-gallrein-2026]]

At the RJC's America 250 gala in Manhattan two weeks later, Brooks called the race "a fight worth having and a victory worth celebrating" and said there "has to be consequences" for Republicans who undermine support for Israel. [[ji-massie-gala-2026]]
